project.title: About this project
paragraphs: This lab was built as direct, hands-on preparation for an internship posting focused on automated air-gap and ransomware isolation for media storage networks — the kind of infrastructure that runs behind a broadcaster's ingest, transcoding and playout pipeline. Rather than studying the topic from the outside, the goal was to build the actual system: a simulated media storage node, a real SIEM watching it, and an automated containment chain triggered by a real detection rule.

Every technical claim on this site is backed by something that actually ran on real hardware: a repurposed 2-core laptop as the SIEM server, a mix of physical machines and VMs across Windows, Linux and macOS, and a genuinely underpowered network that forced real engineering trade-offs instead of clean textbook ones.

The scope grew past the original 17-phase plan once the core detection-and-response chain was working: a full CVE vulnerability-management campaign (24 real CVEs, each with a documented fix/mitigate/accept decision), an 8-sensor Suricata network rollout after discovering a real visibility blind spot, and a complete TheHive + Cortex case-management layer wired directly into Wazuh.

Nothing here uses real malware. Every ransomware-behavior test is a safe file rename or a scoped OpenSSL encryption test on disposable data, always with a backup taken first and a documented restore step. The automation itself was built with a REPORT_ONLY safety flag and never flipped to live-action mode until validated across many events with zero false positives.

approach.title: How this was learned, not just built
approach.intro: Every unfamiliar area — networking APIs, IR frameworks, Ansible internals — was studied on a fixed weekly rhythm before being built, not figured out ad hoc while building.

roadmap.focus: Linux fundamentals — permissions, systemd, LVM, Netplan
Networking I — TCP/IP, VLANs, SDN concepts
SIEM/SOAR concepts and the MITRE ATT&CK framework
Python for automation — hashlib, json, pathlib, subprocess, requests
Network APIs — NETCONF vs SNMP vs CLI/REST, NAPALM/Netmiko/ncclient
Ansible — playbooks, idempotence, and Active Response internals
Incident response — the NIST SP 800-61 cycle, forensic report structure

approach.rhythm: Roughly one hour of theory plus two hours of hands-on practice per weekday, with a standing habit of recording a short demo video every Friday.
approach.pitchTitle: The 3-minute way to explain this project

pitch.text: A media pipeline needs automated ransomware detection and containment without disrupting the live broadcast signal.
A real SIEM (Wazuh) watches a simulated media storage node; a custom rule fires a Python automation chain: isolate, fail over, forensic report — all sharing one incident ID.
3.00s average detection-to-report latency across 10 real runs, 0 false positives — plus a real data-loss bug found and fixed under a 100-file burst load test.
Tested on 2-core hardware with real throughput ceilings; REPORT_ONLY mode never flipped to live action; next step would be extending validation to sustained multi-hour load.
